Shimosuwa Town, accessed February 11, 2021.</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.town.shimosuwa.lg.jp/www/contents/1496969553133/files/5-106.pdf |title=Municipal Cultural Property No. 34 |access-date=2023/8/20 |publisher=Shimosuwa Town}}</ref> It is situated across the {{ill|Togawa River|ja|砥川}} from the {{ill|Suwa-taisha|ja|諏訪大社#下社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Suwa Taisha Shimosha Spring Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q218813}}. The local area name "Sekibutsu" is derived from this statue.

The stone Buddha gained national recognition in the {{ill|1970s|en|1970s|qid=Q35014|lt=1970s}} when it was introduced by the artist {{ill|Tarō Okamoto|en|Tarō Okamoto|qid=Q983942|lt=Taro Okamoto}}.<ref name=kanko>[https://shimosuwaonsen.jp/万治の石仏/ Manji no Sekibutsu] - Shimosuwa Tourism Association, accessed February 11, 2021.</ref>

"Manji no Sekibutsu" is also a registered trademark owned by the Shimosuwa Chamber of Commerce.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.j-platpat.inpit.go.jp/c1800/TR/JP-1975-111530/F9955187CD2A8CF63F94F7E0BFD8C0A6B6A2FE9ED1871582677DE84CB61BA02A/40/ja |title=Trademark Registration No. 1326194 |access-date=2023/7/8 |publisher=National Center for Industrial Property Information and Training}}</ref>

== Overview ==
[[File:Manji-no sekibutsu (stone buddha) , 万治の石仏 - panoramio (20).jpg|thumb|Inscription "Namu Amida Butsu Manji 3rd Year, 11th Month, 1st Day, Ganshu Myōyo Jokō, Shinyo Hiroharu"]]

The stone Buddha measures 2.6 meters in height, 3.8 meters in width, and 3.7 meters in depth. It is made of andesite (hornblende-pyroxene andesite), with a Buddha head approximately 65 centimeters tall placed on a massive stone body.<ref name=kanko/><ref name=":4" /> The front of the body features a carved {{ill|Amitābha|en|Amitābha|qid=Q236242|lt=Amida Nyorai}} seated in {{ill|Mudra|ar|المودرا|bcl|Mudra|bg|Мудра|bn|মুদ্রা (ভঙ্গিমা)|ca|Mudra|cs|Mudra|cy|Mwdra|de|Mudra|es|Mudra|et|Mudra|eu|Mudra|fa|مودرا|fi|Mudra|fr|Mudra|gl|Mudra|he|מודרה|hi|मुद्रा (भाव भंगिमा)|hu|Mudrá|hy|Մուդրա|id|Mudrā|it|Mudra|ja|印相|jv|Mudra|ka|მუდრა|kk|Мудра|km|មុទ្រា|kn|ಮುದ್ರೆ (ಭಾರತೀಯ ಧರ್ಮ)|ko|인상 (종교)|lt|Mudra|ml|മുദ്ര|mr|मुद्रा|ms|Mudra|my|မုဒြာ|ne|मुद्रा (भावभङ्गी)|nl|Mudra|nn|Mudra|no|Mudrā|or|ମୁଦ୍ରା (ପୂଜା)|pl|Mudra|pt|Mudra|ro|Mudra|ru|Мудра|simple|Mudra|sk|Mudrá|sr|Мудра|sv|Mudra|ta|முத்திரை (பரதநாட்டியம்)|te|ముద్ర|th|มุทรา|tl|Mudra|tr|Mudra|tt|Мудра|uk|Мудра|vi|Thủ ấn|zh|手印|qid=Q208030|lt=Dhyanamudra}}.<ref name=town/><ref name=":4" />

The robe is adorned with symbols such as {{ill|Swastika|en|Swastika|qid=Q45513|lt=Swastika}} (right-facing), the sun, thunder, clouds, rocks, and the moon, reflecting esoteric {{ill|Mikkyō|en|Mikkyō|qid=Q336102|lt=Mikkyō}} mandalas. These elements are attributed to the "One Body, Two Buddhas" doctrine of a sect of sculpting priests from the {{ill|Jōdo-shū|en|Jōdo-shū|qid=Q912208|lt=Jōdo-shū}}, combining {{ill|Amitābha|en|Amitābha|qid=Q236242|lt=Amida Nyorai}} with {{ill|Vairocana|en|Vairocana|qid=Q239847|lt=Dainichi Nyorai}}.<ref name=town/><ref name=":4" />

== Legend ==
A local legend recounts that during the construction of a large {{ill|Torii|en|Torii|qid=Q234731|lt=torii}} for Suwa Taisha in {{ill|1657|en|1657|qid=Q6987|lt=1657}} (Meireki 3), a stonecutter attempted to use the current stone Buddha as material. However, upon striking it with a chisel, the stone bled. Afraid of divine retribution, the construction ceased. The stone was later consecrated as an Amida Nyorai.<ref name=town/><ref name=kanko/>
